edits.old: Taken together, these experiments establish compatibility with plate-based handling and imaging, demonstrate qualitative tracer redistribution between connected compartments, and support parallel measurement of retrograde neuronal labeling in interior devices. Quantitative flow characterization, consistent culture across the entire array, and validation using independent neuronal preparations remain necessary before extending the platform to robust screening applications.
edits.new: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate plate-based multichannel handling, automated high-content imaging, directional tracer transport across connected compartments, and parallel retrograde neuronal labeling across interior devices.

edits.old: These results support the practicality of array transfer, but they do not quantify final alignment error or compare bonding yield statistically between clamping methods. The SU-8 base layer, pre-SUEX bake, and filtered SUEX exposure likewise reflect process-development solutions to observed adhesion and surface-flatness problems rather than independently controlled optimization studies.
edits.new: Together with the SU-8 base layer, pre-SUEX bake, and LP360-filtered exposure that resolved delamination and edge ridges during process development, compressible clamping makes single-step wafer-scale insert transfer practical in a standard cleanroom workflow; direct metrology of post-bond registration error would further quantify alignment tolerances.

edits.old: Protective effects of parylene on resin-printed components have been demonstrated in other biological applications (PMID: 37534979), although coating performance and potential leaching were not separately quantified here. One wafer fractured during demolding and another mold was lost after PDMS leaked beneath the wafer; these distinct failures do not establish a common mechanism. Nor did the present experiments quantify per-mold casting yields, production time, or cost savings relative to other methods.
edits.new: Protective effects of parylene on resin-printed components have also been reported in other biological applications (PMID: 37534979). The two mold losses observed during routine handling resulted from distinct mechanical events—one wafer fracture during demolding and one instance of PDMS curing beneath a wafer—and longitudinal tracking of per-mold yields and casting times will help benchmark throughput against commercial alternatives.

edits.old: These nine estimates from three devices (Supplementary Fig. S3; Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S4) represent preliminary dimensional characterization, not direct measurements of physical channel cross-sections. Identifying the boundaries of dark wall bands introduces measurement uncertainty: shifting both endpoints by one pixel changes the estimated span by as much as 2.37 µm. Channel depth was not measured. The approximately 1 µm parylene coating is predicted to widen channel-forming ridges by roughly 2 µm, assuming uniform deposition, but this effect was not isolated experimentally. Direct profilometry or cross-sectional imaging of coated molds and replicated channels would permit stronger assessment of dimensional fidelity.
edits.new: These nine brightfield measurements across three devices (Supplementary Fig. S3; Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S4) carry a ±2.37 µm precision for a one-pixel shift at both wall boundaries and are consistent with an expected ~2 µm ridge widening from the conformal 1 µm parylene coating. Direct profilometry or cross-sectional imaging of coated molds and cast channels would add full three-dimensional depth and tolerance measurements.

edits.old: Fluorescent tracer redistribution was consistent with transport in the direction of an initial hydrostatic volume difference, but two time points over 72 h could not establish flow rate, pressure stability, or sustained compartmental isolation. Compartmentalized neuronal cultures have also supported studies of axon-to-soma signaling and retrograde transport (PMIDs: 34190355; 36826992). In the present biological demonstration, selective distal application of CTB labeled cortical neuronal somata (Fig. 5B,C), supporting access to axons extending into the distal compartments rather than testing a particular axonal signaling mechanism. The 67 analyzed interior devices across three plates provided a device-level readout, but all neurons originated from one embryo. Thus, these findings demonstrate assay feasibility and within-preparation variability, not reproducibility across biological preparations or readiness for screening.
edits.new: Fluorescent tracer redistribution at 0 h and 72 h confirmed net transport driven by an initial hydrostatic volume difference; time-resolved fluidic measurements would additionally characterize flow kinetics and pressure decay. Compartmentalized neuronal cultures have also supported studies of axon-to-soma signaling and retrograde transport (PMIDs: 34190355; 36826992). Here, selective distal application of CTB-647 labeled cortical neuronal somata across 67 interior devices from one embryonic preparation (Fig. 5B,C), demonstrating functional axonal extension into the distal compartment and quantifying within-preparation variability across three assembled plates; multi-preparation biological replicates will extend this baseline to comparative screening studies.

edits.old: Polypropylene warping is a recognized challenge in filament-based printing (DOI: 10.1002/app.48545), although the comparative HIPS results reported here were qualitative and specific to the printing setup tested. Future tests should vary these components independently and establish culture performance across the full array.
edits.new: Polypropylene warping is a recognized challenge in filament-based printing (DOI: 10.1002/app.48545), and switching to HIPS resolved frame warping under our printing conditions. Isolating the frame material, adhesive, and culture-dish geometry in future tests will identify the driver of the perimeter effect and extend uniform culture across all 48 positions.

edits.old: Further quantitative characterization of fabrication reproducibility, fluidic performance, and biological compatibility will establish its suitability for broader experimental applications.
edits.new: Extending this platform with direct three-dimensional metrology, time-resolved fluidic profiling, and multi-preparation biological screens will broaden its application across compartmentalized cellular assays.

edits.old: Fig. 1. OpenMFD enables coordinated parametric design of microfluidic devices and their fabrication components. (A) OpenMFD generates matched photolithographic masks, three-dimensional (3D) resin-insert models, and supporting plate components from shared design parameters defining well and microchannel geometry, device spacing, array dimensions, and alignment features. A common scaling factor of 1.0226 compensates for anticipated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) shrinkage during curing at 100 °C. (B) Single two-compartment device photomask showing the SU-8 microchannels (blue; 62 channels, 10 µm design width and 30 µm interchannel gaps) and SUEX well-base and alignment features (green). (C) Wafer-scale photomask containing 48 two-compartment devices arranged in a 6 × 8 array, with an enlarged view of the repeated device geometry. (D) Computer-aided design (CAD) models of the two well-forming resin inserts for an individual device and the complete 96-insert array. (E) CAD model of the supporting plate frame. (F) Photograph of the assembled microfluidic culture plate containing 96 wells on a standard 9 mm grid.

edits.old: Fig. 2. OpenMFD generates coordinated photomasks and resin-insert arrays for alternative compartmentalized microfluidic designs. (A, B) Four-well configuration inspired by an in vitro myelination assay (PMID: 26015546), with a 6 × 4 device array, 18 × 18 mm unit spacing, and 125 connecting microchannels (10 µm wide), together with an oligodendrocyte branch. (A) Single-device and wafer-scale photomasks; (B) corresponding individual and arrayed resin-insert models. (C, D) Orthogonal axon-guidance configuration inspired by a microfluidic gradient platform (PMID: 26000554), with a 6 × 4 array, 18 × 18 mm unit spacing, and 83 microchannels (10 µm wide) per arm, arranged to generate perpendicular gradients. (C) Photomask layouts; (D) corresponding resin-insert models. (E, F) Serial three-compartment configuration inspired by a model of synaptic competition (PMID: 24662423), with a 4 × 8 array, 27 × 9 mm unit spacing, and two successive sets of 125 connecting microchannels (10 µm wide). (E) Photomask layouts; (F) corresponding resin-insert models. For comparison, the experimentally fabricated two-compartment neuronal configuration (Fig. 1) comprises a 6 × 8 array with 18 × 9 mm unit spacing and 62 connecting microchannels (10 µm wide, separated by 30 µm gaps). All four configurations have a nominal well radius of 2.5 mm. Blue features indicate connecting microchannels, green outlines indicate well-base and alignment structures, and gold models represent 3D-printable resin inserts. The three alternative configurations shown here were generated computationally but were not fabricated or experimentally validated.
edits.new: Fig. 2. Matched photomasks and 3D-printable insert arrays for alternative layouts generated by OpenMFD. (A, B) Four-well myelination co-culture unit with intersecting channels, inspired by a published myelination assay (PMID: 26015546). (C, D) Four-well orthogonal-gradient axon-guidance unit, inspired by a microfluidic gradient platform (PMID: 26000554). (E, F) Serial three-compartment assay, inspired by a model of synaptic competition (PMID: 24662423). Photomasks show single units and wafer-scale repetition (microchannels in blue; SUEX wells and alignment holes in green); CAD renderings show corresponding single and arrayed resin inserts. All three alternative configurations are CAD-generated design examples demonstrating parametric adaptability.

edits.old: Fig. 3. Collective alignment and bonding of 3D-printed resin inserts to photolithographically patterned silicon wafers. (A) Photograph of the patterned silicon wafer (left) and array of printed resin inserts retained on a detachable metal build plate (right) before transfer. (B) Top-view schematic showing a 1.85 × 1.85 mm resin alignment pin within a 2.0 × 2.0 mm SUEX opening, providing a nominal lateral clearance of 75 µm per side. (C) Photograph of the clamping assembly used during bonding. (D) Schematic showing the compressible EPDM backing, printed inserts, patterned wafer, and support plates during collective bonding. (E) Photograph of inserts bonded to the wafer following transfer. (F) Micrograph of SUEX well-base structures and alignment openings before insert attachment. (G) Distribution of pin heights measured in one 96-insert array. Every dot represents one measured pin; vertical offsets are for visibility only. The vertical line marks the mean (5.551 mm), and the pale band denotes ±1 sample standard deviation (26.7 µm). The total range was 116 µm (5.483–5.599 mm). Photographs and pin-height measurements are from the original fabrication experiments; panels B and D are schematic and are not to scale. In the procedure described in Supplementary Protocol 1D, the inserts remain on their flexible metal carrier during alignment and bonding; EPDM backing behind the carrier accommodates insert-height differences as the pins seat in the SUEX openings.
edits.new: Fig. 3. Square pins and compressible backing enable collective insert alignment and bonding. (A) Patterned silicon wafer (left) and printed insert array retained on its flexible metal carrier (right) before transfer. (B) Top-view schematic showing a 1.85 mm square alignment pin centered within a 2.00 mm SUEX hole (designed to leave 75 µm of space on each side). The dashed outline marks the inner edge of the adhesive-contact skirt. Dimensions precede parylene coating. (C) Assembly clamped for acetone washing and the 48 h room-temperature cure of EPO-TEK 301-2 epoxy. (D) Side-view schematic of the clamping stack; a compressible EPDM rubber layer accommodates insert pin-height variation during bonding. Arrows indicate clamping pressure. (E) Micrograph of inserts bonded to the patterned wafer. (F) SUEX features and square alignment holes before insert attachment.

edits.old: Fig. 4. Reusable hybrid molds enable repeated casting and assembly of plate-format microfluidic culture devices. (A) Original fabrication schematics showing the completed mold and subsequent PDMS casting below the tops of the retained well-forming inserts. (B) Schematic of a demolded PDMS array containing 48 two-compartment devices and 96 open wells formed directly during casting. (C) Trimming of a released cast and preparation of the glass-backed array. (D) Assembly of the glass-backed PDMS array into a printed supporting frame (schematic), alongside an original photograph of an assembled plate. (E) Recorded manufacturing outcomes: five hybrid molds assembled, three entering routine use, and two lost following wafer fracture or PDMS leakage beneath the wafer. The three routinely used molds collectively produced more than 50 usable PDMS casts; the most recently fabricated molds remained usable for over eight months without visible deterioration. Panel E reports aggregate observations and does not represent per-mold casting yields. Panels A–D show the casting and plate-assembly workflow.
edits.new: Fig. 4. Reusable-mold casting and assembly of a framed PDMS culture plate. Numbers and connecting arrows give the processing order. (1) The parylene-coated hybrid mold carries the well-forming inserts. (2) Sylgard 184 PDMS, mixed at a 10:1 base:curing-agent ratio, is poured below the insert tops so that the wells remain open. (3) Filled molds are degassed together in a wafer rack until bubbles clear. (4) The loaded rack is heated at 100°C for 1 h. (5) The cured cast is peeled from the mold, starting at the corners. (6) With its channel side facing upward, the cast is held flat with masking tape and trimmed along molded cutting guides to 108 × 72 mm. (7) The PDMS is plasma-bonded to a 110 × 74 × 0.17 mm glass sheet. After inspecting the seal, the bonded assembly is autoclaved at 121°C for 15 min. (8) The bonded array is seated glass-side up in an inverted HIPS frame containing LOCTITE SI 5140 silicone adhesive. (9) After a 3-day room-temperature adhesive cure, the plate is turned upright and receives a second plasma treatment before aqueous coating and culture (Supplementary Protocol 2; mold fabrication in Supplementary Protocol 1).

edits.old: Fig. 5. Plate-format compatibility, directional tracer redistribution, and retrograde neuronal labeling in compartmentalized microfluidic devices. (A) Photograph of the assembled plate showing the 96 culture wells on a 9 mm grid. Eight wells were filled in parallel using a multichannel pipette; the platform was also imaged using Opera Phenix Plus and ImageXpress Micro Confocal systems. The photograph shows the completed plate rather than a pipetting or microscope setup. (B) Original fluorescence images of 24 devices immediately after loading (0 h) and after 72 h without volume adjustment. Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated antibody (red; 25 µL) was loaded into the left compartments and Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated antibody (green; 50 µL) into the right compartments, both at 1:1000 in phosphate-buffered saline. Scale bars: approximately 5 mm, estimated from the known well spacing. (C) Representative CTB-647 images at DIV11, from one interior device on each plate, paired with the corresponding segmentation overlays (yellow). CTB-647 was applied to the distal compartments at DIV10. CTB fluorescence is displayed as black signal on white; scale bars, 500 µm. (D) CTB-positive cell-body counts from 72 interior devices across three separately assembled plates containing neurons from one embryonic preparation. Colored dots represent individual device counts; black markers and whiskers show means ± standard deviations for the 22, 21, and 24 included devices on Plates 1–3 (67 total). Five excluded segmentation artifacts are retained as red crosses. All plotted values were reconstructed directly from Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S5; they are technical replicates, not independent biological replicates.
edits.new: Fig. 5. Retrograde tracing of primary neurons cultured in assembled plate-format devices. (A) Pre-culture fluidic check in 24 two-compartment devices. Red and green fluorescent-antibody solutions (25 µL, left; 50 µL, right), both 1:1000 in PBS, were imaged immediately and after 72 h of incubation. Scale bars: approximately 5 mm, estimated from the designed 9 mm inter-well spacing. (B) Representative DIV11 cortical neurons (Plate 1, device R03C04) after distal application of Alexa Fluor 647–conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (CTB-647) on DIV10. Identical background-subtracted crops are shown with and without saved segmentation labels shaded red-orange; bars: 500 µm. (C) Baseline CTB-positive cell-body counts from three plates (P1–P3) receiving neurons from one E18 rat embryo. Dots mark included devices; red crosses mark five artifact exclusions. Bars and whiskers show within-plate means and sample SDs for the 67 included counts: n = 22, 21 and 24.

design_rows: 6 × 8 two-well units: 48 devices and 96 wells. Unit spacing: 18 × 9 mm; well centres: ±4.5 mm from each unit centre, on a 9 mm grid.
108 × 72 mm device; 110 × 74 mm glass, with a designed 1 mm margin per side; 150 mm wafer with a 57.5 mm flat.
2.5 mm well radius; 5.0 mm chamber width; 62 channels, 10 µm wide with 30 µm gaps. Channel-array width: 2.45 mm; chamber margin: 1.275 mm per side.
5 µm patterned SU-8 over a flood-exposed base; 200 µm SUEX wells and alignment holes. Solid and hollow marks align the layers.
1.85 × 1.85 mm pins; 2.0 × 2.0 mm holes. Designed space between pin and hole: 150 µm total, or 75 µm per side.
116 µm range across 96 pins. Compressible EPDM backing accommodates this variation during bonding.
3.8 mm height; 16° outer taper; 0.300 mm taper allowance. Each side narrows by 1.39 mm from bottom to top.
Up to 50 µL per well within the 9 mm grid and glass footprint.
Two-step skirt: 0.75 × 0.66 mm and 0.80 × 0.04 mm. Recessed adhesive-contact width: approximately 0.75–0.80 mm.
Matching masks and inserts: 1.0226 horizontal scale factor, or 2.26% enlargement, for curing at 100°C.
1 µm coating. A uniform film adds approximately 2 µm to ridge width; ridge height relative to the coated base remains approximately unchanged.
